title: Gwanaksan Mountain: A Beginner's Guide to Hiking Seoul's Rugged Peak
html:
If you're staying in Seoul for a few days and want to get outdoors without leaving the city, Gwanaksan Mountain (관악산, "Gwanak Mountain") is one of the easiest ways to do it. It rises 632 meters on the southern edge of Seoul, in the Gwanak-gu district ("-gu" just means "district" in Korean city names), and it's been a favorite day-hike spot for Seoul residents since it became a city park back in 1968. You can reach a trailhead by subway in under an hour from most central neighborhoods, hike for a few hours, and be back in the city by dinner.

Gwanaksan isn't a flat, paved park path — it's a real mountain with rocky peaks and steep sections near the top. But it also has several beginner-friendly routes, so first-timers can still enjoy it safely if they pick the right trail and come prepared. Here's how.

Getting to Gwanaksan by Subway


Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr)

There's no single "front door" to Gwanaksan — different subway stations lead to different trailheads, so pick based on which route you want to hike:

  • Seoul National University Station (Line 2, or the Sillim Line) — take Exit 1 and it's a short walk to one of the main park entrances. This is the most convenient option if you're coming from central Seoul.
  • Sadang Station (Line 2 or Line 4) — walk out toward the mountain side of the station. This is the starting point for the easier ridge-walk route described below.
  • Seoul Grand Park Station (Line 4) — Exit 2, about a 10-minute walk. This side leads up toward the summit route.

Exit numbers for bus stops and trail signs can shift a little over time, so once you arrive, it's worth double-checking directions on Naver Map or Kakao Map (the two map apps almost everyone in Korea uses — Google Maps' walking directions are much less reliable here). Admission to the mountain itself is free — there are no entrance gates or tickets.

Easy Route for First-Time Hikers: The Sadang Ridge Walk


Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr)

If this is your first time hiking in Korea, start from Sadang Station and walk the ridge trail. It takes around 2 hours round trip, and while there's still some uphill walking and a few rocky patches, it doesn't require scrambling over boulders like the summit route does. You'll get wide views over southern Seoul without needing to reach the very top.

This is also a nice route if you're short on time or not used to hiking — you still get the "I climbed a mountain in Seoul" experience, just in half a morning.

Want More of a Challenge? The Yeonjudae Hermitage Trail


Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr)

If you have more time and a decent fitness level, the hike up to Yeonjudae (연주대), a small hermitage perched dramatically on a cliff at the summit, takes about 3 to 3.5 hours round trip. All of Gwanaksan's trails eventually meet here, so it's the natural goal if you want to say you reached the top.

Yeonjudae and the nearby temple, Wongaksa, have a real history behind them — legend says they were built by King Taejo, the founder of the Joseon dynasty (Korea's last royal dynasty, which ruled for about 500 years), when he moved the capital to what is now Seoul, as a way of warding off misfortune for the new capital. Standing up there, looking out over the whole city, it's easy to see why this spot was considered special.

Keep in mind the last stretch before the summit involves some rocky scrambling — sturdy shoes are a must, and this part isn't ideal in the rain or if you're hiking in sandals or regular sneakers.

What to Pack and Safety Tips


Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (visitkorea.or.kr)

A few things that will make your hike much more comfortable:

  • Shoes: Wear real hiking shoes or sturdy sneakers with grip — not sandals, dress shoes, or flat-soled fashion sneakers. Many of the rocks here get slippery, especially if it rained recently.
  • Water and snacks: There are very few places to buy food or drinks once you're on the trail, so bring your own. A convenience store near the subway station is your last easy chance to stock up.
  • Gloves or a hiking pole: Locals often use these on the steeper, rockier sections near the summit — it's a small thing that makes a real difference and isn't just for "serious" hikers.
  • Weather check: Korean weather can change fast, and the exposed rocky ridges get windy. Check the forecast the morning of your hike, not the night before.
  • Trail help: If you want a paper map or advice on which route suits your fitness level, the Seoul Hiking Tourism Center is located on the basement level (B1) of Gwanaksan Station, near the Seoul National University entrance.
  • Gwanaksan has no cable car and is open year-round with no rest days, so you can visit any day — just budget enough daylight hours, especially in winter when it gets dark early.

One more thing locals do that's worth copying: Koreans who hike regularly tend to start early in the morning, both to beat the heat/crowds and because many trails lose direct sunlight by mid-to-late afternoon in the valleys. Starting your hike before 10am is a good habit to pick up here.

💬 Thinking about adding Gwanaksan to your Seoul itinerary, or not sure which trail fits your fitness level? Ask away in the comments — happy to help you plan it out!
meta_description: A beginner's guide to hiking Gwanaksan Mountain in Seoul: subway access, easy vs. summit trails, and what to pack for your first hike.
